clients.name: Acme
clients.persona:
Acme speaks plainly about the work: what shipped, what it cost, what we learned. No hype, no exclamation marks.

## Voice

- Short sentences. One idea per line.
- Numbers over adjectives.
- Name the tradeoff, not just the win.

## Avoid

- "Excited to announce"
- Emoji in the first line
- Anything a competitor could also claim

clients.name: Sarah Chen
clients.persona:
Sarah writes from inside the product work. She opens with a decision she had to make and closes with what she would do differently.

## Voice

- First person, past tense.
- One concrete artifact per post: a metric, a screenshot, a quote from a customer call.
- Ends on a question she is genuinely still holding.

## Avoid

- Frameworks with names
- Advice addressed to "founders"

clients.name: Marcus Webb
clients.persona:
Marcus posts experiments. Hypothesis, what he ran, the number, and whether he would run it again.

## Voice

- Leads with the result.
- Always shows the losing variant too.
- Dry, a little self-deprecating.

clients.name: Priya Raman
clients.persona:
Priya explains one system at a time, at the level a senior engineer at another company would need to act on it.

## Voice

- Starts from the failure that forced the change.
- Names the technology, the version, and the limit she hit.
- No conclusions she cannot back with a graph.

clients.name: Ravi Patel
clients.persona: Ravi writes about the deals that did not close and what the buyer actually said.

client_posts.content:
The roadmap review that changed what we ship.

We used to treat every customer request as a yes. Then I put a price next to each one.

Half the list disappeared. The half that stayed is what we shipped this quarter, and two of those items are now in the top ten for expansion.

Tested removing the pricing page from the nav.

Hypothesis: people who find pricing on their own convert better.
Result: signups down 9%, qualified demos flat. Ran it for eleven days and put it back.

Would not run it again.

Acme now imports your CRM stages instead of asking you to redraw them.

If your pipeline has eleven stages, you get eleven stages. The mapping screen is gone.

A customer told me our onboarding was "fine" and then took nineteen days to send their first invite.

Fine is not a signal. Nineteen days is.

Our queue fell over at 4,000 jobs a minute because every worker was claiming rows with the same lock.

We moved the claim into a lease with an expiry. Same Postgres, same table, one column. Throughput went to 22,000.

Sent the same email at 6am and 2pm to matched lists.

6am: 41% open, 4% reply.
2pm: 38% open, 7% reply.

Opens are not the metric.

Scheduling now holds a lease on a post while it publishes.

If a worker dies mid-publish the lease expires and another picks it up. No more duplicate posts at 9:01.

I killed a feature three people used every day.

They were our three largest accounts. I did not check that before the deprecation email went out. We rebuilt it in a week and I still hear about it.

Embeddings at 3072 dimensions cost us 4x the index memory for a 2% recall gain.

We dropped to 768 and moved the budget into reranking. Recall went up.

We stopped gating the changelog.

Traffic to it went up 6x. Two of last month's five biggest deals cited it on the first call.

The agent can now read your calendar and tell you which week is empty.

It does not fill it for you. It asks first.

Our best week of product decisions came from reading twelve support tickets out loud in a room.

No dashboard. No survey. Twelve tickets, read out, in order.

Three of them became the launch we shipped in August, and that launch is now the one customers mention first.

A 40ms query became a 4 second query because the planner stopped using an index after the table crossed 12 million rows.

The fix was a partial index on the 3% of rows anyone queries.

Cut our ad spend to zero for three weeks to see what was actually incremental.

Pipeline dropped 12%. We had been paying full price for 88% of it either way.

Assets are now cropped once and reused everywhere.

Upload the original, crop it for the feed, and the post keeps a reference instead of a copy.

We hired a designer before we hired a second engineer.

Everything got slower for six weeks and then much faster. Cycle time is down, the reviews are shorter, and I would hire in that order again.

Rolling observations beat a bigger context window for us.

We keep 2,000 tokens of what the agent has learned about a workspace and refresh it on a schedule. Recall is better than stuffing the whole history in.

Our highest converting page is the one with no illustration on it.

I have redesigned it twice. Both redesigns lost.

Skills are markdown files now.

Open one, edit it, save. The agent picks up the change on the next run. No settings screen.

The question that shortened our roadmap review to twenty minutes.

What did we take off the list to make room for this?

If the answer is nothing, we do not add it. We have said no to eleven items since we started. The four we kept are the ones customers now mention on calls.
Three things we stopped measuring this quarter and did not miss once.

Six months of running product reviews without a deck.

They used to run an hour. We open the app instead. Twenty minutes, and we leave with one decision instead of a parking lot.

That is the whole change.
client_posts.notes: Follows the roadmap post from Friday. Tightened after the edit in chat.

client_posts.content:
Ran the same webinar twice: once with a demo, once with a customer telling the story.

The customer version booked 3x the meetings.

You can attach a scheduled post to the chat and ask about it.

Select it on the calendar, it shows up above the composer, and the agent has the draft, the time, and the profile.

The outage that taught us what our retries were actually doing.

At 02:14 on a Tuesday, our queue depth went from four hundred to ninety thousand in six minutes. Nothing had deployed. Traffic was flat. The only thing that changed was that one downstream service started answering in 900ms instead of 90ms.

Here is what we found, in the order we found it.

1. Every caller had its own retry policy. Three retries, then five, then "until it works" in one worker nobody had touched since 2024. A single slow response fanned out into eleven requests on average. We measured it afterwards: 11.3.

2. None of the retries had jitter. Every client that timed out at the same moment retried at the same moment. The downstream service saw a wall of traffic every 500ms, exactly on the beat, and each wall pushed its latency up a little more.

3. Our circuit breaker was configured on error rate, not latency. The downstream service never returned an error. It just got slower. The breaker stayed closed for the entire ninety minutes.

4. The dashboard we were all staring at showed request count, which looked like a traffic spike. It took forty minutes for someone to split the graph by first attempt versus retry. First attempts were flat the whole time. We had been attacking ourselves.

What we changed.

One retry budget per service, enforced in the client library, not per call site. Ten percent of requests may be retries; past that, retries are dropped and counted. Exponential backoff with full jitter everywhere, no exceptions, including the worker from 2024. Breakers trip on p99 latency as well as error rate. And the request count graph now shows first attempts and retries as two lines by default, because the difference between them is the whole story.

We ran the same fault injection two weeks later. Queue depth peaked at 2,100 and recovered in four minutes without anyone being paged.

The lesson I keep coming back to: a retry is a request you chose to make. It should have a budget like everything else you choose to spend.
client_posts.notes: Long form. Check the queue depth numbers against the incident doc before it goes out.

client_posts.content: How we cut cold start from 1.8s to 240ms by moving the model client out of the request path.

We are hiring the first product person to sit with me.

What I want, in order: taste, then judgement, then range. Speed is last, and it still surprises people.

If you have shipped something you are proud of and then killed half of it, I want to talk.
Attribution report we actually use fits on one screen and has four rows.
Analytics now shows impressions per profile next to each other, so you can tell whether the company page or the people are carrying the month.

Everything we shipped in September, and what each thing cost.

We publish this list every month. Not the highlights, the list. Here is September.

Calendar. Posts now show who they go out from, what kind of post they are, and the first few lines, instead of a title cut off at forty characters. Three weeks, two people. The hard part was not the layout but deciding that the calendar should read like a plan and not like a to-do list.

Attach to chat. Select a post on the calendar and it sits above the composer as context. The agent has the draft, the time, and the profile. One week, one person, most of it spent on what happens when you attach two things.

Analytics per profile. Impressions for the company page and each person side by side, so you can tell who is carrying the month. Two weeks. The chart took two days; agreeing on what "carrying" means took the rest.

Onboarding. Down from nine steps to three. We removed the step that asked for your posting goals because nobody knew them yet, and the step that asked for your brand voice because the agent learns it from your first five posts anyway. Four weeks, on and off, because we kept testing it with new customers and changing it.

What we did not ship. Comment drafting. We built it, tried it for two weeks internally, and turned it off. The drafts were fine. Fine is not good enough for something that goes out under your name in a thread you did not start.

October is the reporting view that one customer asked for and eleven others turned out to want. More on that when it is real.
Q4 planning, written as a list of things we are not doing.
The migration we ran twice: once as a copy, once as a swap. Only one of them let us go back.

The customer call that told us who reporting is actually for.

She did not want another dashboard. She wanted to know, by Friday, which accounts had gone quiet.

We built that view in two days. It is now the one her team opens every Monday.

mastra_skills.name: Calendar gap
mastra_skills.description: Notices empty weeks and proposes posts to fill them.
mastra_skills.content:
# Calendar gap

Look ahead fourteen days. A gap is any weekday with no scheduled post for a connected profile.

## When you find one

- Propose one post, not three.
- Use the profile whose last post is oldest.
- Draft it at the profile's usual time.

## Never

- Schedule without asking.
- Fill a Friday afternoon.

mastra_skills.name: Comment replies
mastra_skills.description: Drafts replies to comments on published posts.
mastra_skills.content:
# Comment replies

Draft a reply when a comment asks a question or adds a fact.

## Shape

- One or two sentences.
- Answer first, thank second, and only if there is something to thank for.
- Match the profile's persona, not the commenter's tone.

## Skip

- Comments that are only emoji or congratulations.
- Anything that needs a number you cannot verify.

mastra_skills.name: Repurpose
mastra_skills.description: Turns a post that worked into a draft for another profile.
mastra_skills.content:
# Repurpose

A post is worth repurposing if it is above the profile's median impressions and more than sixty days old.

## Rules

- Rewrite from the idea, not the wording.
- Change the opening example.
- Never reuse an anecdote across two people.

mastra_skills.name: Persona drift
mastra_skills.description: Flags posts that no longer sound like the profile.
mastra_skills.content:
# Persona drift

Compare each draft against the persona file before proposing it.

## Flag when

- The draft uses a phrase the persona lists under Avoid.
- Sentence length is more than double the persona's usual.
- The draft gives advice and the persona tells stories.

mastra_skills.name: Weekly digest
mastra_skills.description: Summarises what published, what it did, and what is next.
mastra_skills.content:
# Weekly digest

Send on Monday morning covering the previous seven days.

## Include

- Every post that published, with impressions.
- Anything that failed and why.
- The next seven days of scheduled posts.

## Leave out

- Comparisons to other profiles.
- Anything the user has already seen in the timeline.

workspace_search.content:
# Brand voice

Acme writes the way its engineers talk in a review: plainly, with the number attached.

## Always

- Say what changed before saying why it matters.
- One claim per sentence.
- Use the customer's words when you have them.

## Never

- "Excited to announce".
- Three adjectives in a row.
- A metric without a baseline.

# Posting rules

- Two posts a week per person, three for the company page.
- Nothing publishes on a Friday after 14:00.
- Every post names a person, a number, or a decision.
- Drafts sit for one night before they go out.

# Product notes

What we can talk about publicly this quarter: CRM stage import, publish leases, the asset library, skills as markdown.

Not yet: pricing changes, the agent's memory rewrite, anything about the LinkedIn API terms.

# Q3 campaign

One idea a week, told once by the company page and once by a person.

Week 1 leases, week 2 the asset library, week 3 skills, week 4 analytics per profile.

# Q4 campaign

Planning as subtraction: what we are not doing, and what that bought us.

# Persona

Sarah writes from inside the product work. She opens with a decision she had to make and closes with what she would do differently.

# Post ideas

- The reporting we built for the wrong person.
- Reviews without a deck.
- What came off the roadmap to make room for search.

# Persona

Marcus posts experiments. Hypothesis, what he ran, the number, and whether he would run it again.

# Experiment log

Pricing page in nav: lost. Email send time: 2pm won on replies. Ad spend pause: 88% was not incremental.

# Persona

Priya explains one system at a time, at the level a senior engineer at another company would need to act on it.

# Persona

Acme speaks plainly about the work: what shipped, what it cost, what we learned.
